Chapter 14
That Which Concerns A Prince On The Subject Of The Art Of War

A prince should have no other goal, thought, or subject of study than war, its rules, and its discipline. This is the only art expected of a ruler. It is so powerful that it not only maintains the power of those born as princes, but often allows private citizens to rise to that rank. On the other hand, when princes think more about luxury than military strength, they lose their states. The quickest way to lose your power is to neglect the art of war. The surest way to gain a state is to master it. Because Francesco Sforza was a skilled warrior, he rose from a private citizen to become the Duke of Milan. His sons avoided the hardships of war, and so they fell from being dukes back down to private citizens. Being unarmed brings you many evils, but worst of all, it makes you despised. A prince must constantly guard against this disgrace, as I will explain later. There is simply no comparison between an armed man and an unarmed one. It is absurd to expect an armed man to willingly obey an unarmed one, or to think an unarmed prince will be safe among armed servants. The armed man will feel contempt, and the unarmed man will feel suspicion. They cannot possibly work well together. Therefore, a prince who does not understand military strategy will suffer many misfortunes. He will never earn the respect of his soldiers, and he will never be able to trust them. A prince must never let his mind wander from the subject of war. During times of peace, he should train even harder than he does in wartime. He can do this in two ways: through physical action and through mental study.

As for physical action, a prince must keep his troops well organized and strictly drilled. He should also constantly go hunting. Hunting hardens the body to physical hardship and teaches him the geography of his territory. He learns how the mountains rise, how the valleys open up, and how the plains are laid out. He studies the nature of local rivers and marshes, paying the closest possible attention to the terrain. This knowledge is useful in two ways. First, he learns the exact layout of his own country, which helps him plan its defense. Second, by studying one landscape, he trains his eye to quickly understand any new territory he might need to explore later. The hills, valleys, plains, rivers, and marshes in Tuscany, for example, share similarities with landscapes in other countries. By studying one region closely, you can easily grasp the terrain of another. A prince who lacks this skill lacks the most essential quality of a military leader. This knowledge teaches him how to ambush the enemy, choose the best campsites, lead his armies on the march, organize battle formations, and besiege towns with maximum advantage.

Historians praise Philopoemen, the leader of the Achaeans, for many things, but above all because he never stopped thinking about military strategy during times of peace. When he was traveling through the countryside with his friends, he would frequently stop and ask them questions. He would say,

If the enemy were positioned on that hill, and our army were down here, who would have the advantage? How could we safely advance to attack them while keeping our formation intact? If we needed to retreat, how should we fall back? And if the enemy retreated, how should we pursue them?

As they walked, he would present every possible scenario an army might face. He would listen to their opinions, state his own views, and back up his arguments with solid reasoning. Because of these constant discussions, when he was finally leading troops in a real war, he never faced an unexpected crisis he could not handle.

To exercise his mind, a prince must read history. He should study the actions of great men, observing exactly how they conducted themselves in war. He must analyze the causes of their victories and defeats, so he can copy their successes and avoid their failures. Above all, he should follow the example of great leaders from the past who chose to imitate legendary heroes who came before them. These leaders kept the achievements and deeds of their role models constantly in mind. It is said that Alexander the Great imitated Achilles, Julius Caesar imitated Alexander, and Scipio imitated Cyrus. Anyone who reads Xenophon's life of Cyrus will clearly see how Scipio's glory came directly from this kind of imitation. They will see how Scipio carefully copied the chastity, kindness, humanity, and generosity that Xenophon attributed to Cyrus. A wise prince must follow these rules. He must never waste his time standing idle during peace. Instead, he must aggressively build up his resources and abilities so they will be ready when hardship strikes. This way, if his fortune suddenly changes, he will be perfectly prepared to withstand her blows.
